title: Obstructions: name what blocks the line
outcomes: Names the pawns or pieces that block a rook's file or a bishop's diagonal, for both sides
Is told that a piece in front of a passed pawn is a blockade, taught in another lesson
Counts attackers and defenders before trying to remove an enemy obstruction

steps.text: An **obstruction** is a pawn or minor piece that blocks the line of a rook, bishop or queen: a file or a diagonal. It can be the enemy's or your own. A **blockade** is different: a piece placed in front of a passed pawn to stop the pawn. To find obstructions, follow each rook, bishop and queen along its line until it meets the first man.

steps.caption: White to move. The black pawn on e5 and the knight on d5 stand on the lines of White's rook and bishop.

line.say: Nxe5: two white pieces attack the pawn and one black piece defends it.
Rxe5: the rook recaptures; White has won a pawn and the rook now looks up the file as far as the bishop on e7.

claims.statement: The rook's line stops at e5.
The engine's first choice is Nxe5.

steps.text: *Rule of thumb:* an enemy obstruction is easier to remove than one of your own, because you can bring many attackers against it. **Count first:** attackers against defenders, including pieces that join after the first capture; the cheapest man should capture first. With more attackers, taking or exchanging the obstruction can open your line. Without them, leave it alone. An obstruction only troubles the side whose line it blocks.

steps.title: Same pawn, one more defender
steps.prompt: Working: the pawn is attacked twice and defended once. Failing: the same position with one more defender. Predict, then check. (A piece standing in front of a passed pawn is a blockade, taught in "Blockading a passed pawn: check the square".)
Before you chose a move in the last positions, did you first follow each long-range piece along its line to the first man, or did you start with captures? Write what you did first.
